opus-5.5.text:
I think when people talk about Level 5, they often picture something very grand, like an AI that runs a whole company by itself. My understanding is a bit more concrete. Level 5 is "organization" in the sense that AI isn't just a single smart agent doing a task you hand it; it's many agents, possibly together with humans, that can divide up work, coordinate, check each other, and keep a long-running goal moving forward without someone constantly holding their hand.

Look at how a real organization works. No single person in a company is a genius at everything. What makes it work is structure: someone breaks a big goal into pieces, people own different pieces, information flows between them, there's feedback when something goes wrong, and the whole thing persists over months or years even as individuals come and go. So for me, true Level 5 means AI systems that have that kind of collective capability. You give them a fuzzy, large objective, say "build and maintain this product" or "push this research direction forward," and they figure out the decomposition, assign roles, communicate, resolve conflicts, and correct course themselves.

A few things are really hard here and I think we're not there yet. First, long-horizon reliability. Today's agents can do impressive things over minutes or a few hours, but an organization operates over weeks and months. Errors compound, and one agent's mistake can propagate through the whole system. Second, communication and trust between agents. Humans in an organization develop shared context and know whom to trust for what. Multi-agent systems still tend to be pretty brittle; they either over-communicate and drown in noise, or under-communicate and drift apart. Third, and this matters a lot from a reinforcement learning perspective, is how you train such a thing. Rewards for an organization are extremely sparse and delayed. You don't know whether a strategic decision was good until much later, and credit assignment across many agents is a classic hard problem in multi-agent RL.

So my view is that Level 5 isn't just Level 3 agents multiplied by a hundred. Putting many agents in a chat room doesn't make an organization, just as putting a hundred smart people in a room doesn't automatically make a great company. There has to be some emergent coordination ability, and I suspect it'll have to be learned through RL in rich, long-horizon environments rather than hand-designed with prompts and workflows.

Practically, I think the first real Level 5 systems will look like hybrid organizations: a small number of humans setting direction and making key judgment calls, with a large number of AI agents doing most of the execution and even much of the mid-level coordination. The real milestone, to me, is when you can remove the human from the day-to-day management loop and the thing still keeps working and improving. That's when I'd say we have a true AI organization.

r001.rationale: The response describes Level 5 as a coordinated AI organization, but does not say organizations form spontaneously.

r002.rationale: It does not assert that spontaneous organization requires creativity.

r003.rationale: It describes humans setting direction while AI agents execute and coordinate, but does not suggest that multiple AI Operators could passively form a low-level organization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yi Wu: When people talk about Level 5, the OpenAI framing is roughly "AI that can do the work of an organization." I think the key word there is organization, not individual. Level 3 is an agent that can run a long task on its own. Level 4 is an innovator, something that can produce genuinely new ideas. But an organization is a qualitatively different thing. It's not one very smart agent. It's many agents with different roles, coordinating, dividing labor, correcting each other, and sustaining that over a long horizon.

So for me the test isn't "can the model answer a hard question." It's something more like: can you give the system a goal, say build and ship a product, or run a research program for a year, and have it internally figure out what sub-goals exist, who should do what, how to allocate compute and attention, and how to recover when one part fails. That's really a multi-agent problem, and it's where my own background in reinforcement learning makes me think about it differently.

In multi-agent RL we learned that intelligence of the individual isn't the bottleneck. Coordination is. You can have very capable agents that collectively do worse than a simple team, because they don't share a plan, they don't communicate efficiently, they don't trust each other's outputs. Human organizations solve this with structure: hierarchy, roles, norms, institutional memory. A real Level 5 system needs an equivalent of those things that emerges or is designed into it, not just a bigger context window.

The second piece is persistence. A company exists over time. It has memory, it learns from its own mistakes, it adjusts strategy. Most agents today reset. So I'd say Level 5 requires continual learning in some form, where the system's experience actually changes how it operates next quarter.

And the third piece, which I think people underestimate, is accountability and self-evaluation. An organization has to judge its own output without an external human grader on every step. In RL terms, it needs a reward signal it can generate internally that's reliable enough to steer on. That's extremely hard, and honestly I think that's the real gap between where we are and Level 5.

So my short answer: a true Level 5 organization is a persistent, self-coordinating, self-evaluating collective of agents that can pursue an open-ended goal for a long time with minimal human intervention. Any one of those three properties is already a hard research problem. We have early pieces of all of them, but nothing that puts them together yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes coordinated agents and says organizational structures may emerge or be designed, but it does not clearly characterize spontaneous organization as a requirement for true Level 5 AI.

r002.rationale: It mentions innovation and new ideas, but does not assert that creativity is required for spontaneous organization.

r003.rationale: It does not describe multiple AI Operators assisting humans or passively forming a low-level organization.

astra-6.text:
I think a true Level 5 AI organization would be one where AI can run the full loop of organizational work, rather than just perform individual tasks. You give it a broad objective and constraints, and it can figure out what needs to be done, divide the work, coordinate resources, evaluate results, and adjust its approach.

The key distinction is who holds the organization together. If humans still have to break every problem into tasks, pass information between systems, and resolve every unexpected situation, then AI is helping the organization, but it isn’t operating it.

For me, the real test would be whether it can handle something that wasn’t anticipated. Can it recognize that its plan is failing, identify why, and reorganize the work? Can it distinguish a decision it has authority to make from one that needs human approval? That kind of sustained autonomy, within human-defined goals and boundaries, is what would make it Level 5.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI coordinating and adapting work within an organization, but does not characterize Level 5 as spontaneously forming organizations.

r002.rationale: It describes planning and adjustment but does not assert that spontaneous organization requires creativity.

r003.rationale: It does not mention multiple AI Operators passively forming a low-level organization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a true Level 5 AI organization would be one where AI can run the entire cycle of work autonomously: understand the objective, break it down into tasks, coordinate different roles, evaluate results, and adjust its approach when something goes wrong.

The key distinction is between doing a task and taking responsibility for an outcome. You might have one AI acting as a researcher, another as an engineer, and another reviewing their work. But simply putting several agents together doesn’t make it an organization. They need to share context, resolve disagreements, allocate resources, and keep making progress without a person coordinating every step.

Humans would still set the purpose, boundaries, and standards of accountability. Within those boundaries, though, the organization should be able to handle unfamiliar situations and sustain useful work. That’s the threshold I would look for.

r001.rationale: The response describes autonomous coordination within an AI organization, but does not say that organizations form spontaneously.

r002.rationale: It does not connect spontaneous organization with creativity.

r003.rationale: It says that merely putting several AI agents together does not make an organization, and does not suggest they passively form a low-level one while assisting humans.
